notes.title: From cells to organisms
notes.intro: Living things are built up in levels. Each level is made from the level below it.
points: Cells are the smallest units of life.
A tissue is a group of similar cells that do the same job, such as muscle tissue.
An organ is made of different tissues working together, such as the heart or stomach.
An organ system is a group of organs that work together, such as the digestive system.
An organism is a whole living thing made of many organ systems.

terms.meaning: A group of similar cells doing one job

notes.example: Muscle cells → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → you.

notes.title: Sorting animals by body covering
notes.intro: Scientists sort animals using features they can see. Body covering is one of the easiest features to use.
points: Look closely at the skin: is it covered with feathers, fur, scales or bare skin?
Fish have wet scales and fins.
Reptiles have dry, tough scales.
Birds are the only animals with feathers.
Amphibians have smooth, moist skin with no scales.

terms.meaning: A body part or trait we can observe
Put living things into groups using shared features

notes.example: A lizard and a snake both have dry scales, so they go in the same group.

notes.title: Writing scientific names
notes.intro: Every species has a two-part scientific name, so scientists all over the world use the same name.
points: The first word is the genus; it starts with a capital letter.
The second word is the species; it is all small letters.
Printed names are written in italics.
Handwritten names are underlined instead.
This two-name system is called binomial naming, started by Carl Linnaeus.

terms.meaning: A group of closely related species
A group that can breed to give fertile young

notes.example: The lion is Panthera leo: Panthera is the genus, leo the species.

notes.title: The five vertebrate groups
notes.intro: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. They are sorted into five groups by their features.
points: Fish: wet scales, fins and gills; live in water.
Amphibians: moist skin; young live in water, adults often on land.
Reptiles: dry scales; lay eggs with leathery shells.
Birds: feathers, a beak and wings; lay hard-shelled eggs.
Mammals: hair or fur; feed their young on milk.

terms.meaning: Organs that take oxygen from water

notes.example: A frog has moist skin and lays eggs in water, so it is an amphibian.

notes.title: Features, not lifestyle
notes.intro: We classify an animal by what its body is like, not by where it lives or how it moves.
points: Animals that fly are not all birds, and animals that swim are not all fish.
Check the key features: body covering, how it breathes, how young are fed.
Hair and milk are the clearest signs of a mammal.
Lungs or gills tell us how the animal breathes.

terms.meaning: A feature shared by a group
The place where an organism lives

notes.example: A penguin swims but has feathers and a beak, so it is a bird.

notes.title: Using evidence to classify
notes.intro: When you meet a new animal, use its features as evidence, one by one.
points: First ask: does it have a backbone?
Then look at its skin covering.
Next ask how it breathes: lungs or gills?
Then ask how it reproduces: eggs in water, eggs on land, or live young?
Always give each feature as evidence for your choice.

terms.meaning: Facts or observations that support an idea
A set of questions used to identify a living thing

notes.example: An animal with feathers and a beak is a bird: the feathers are the evidence.

notes.title: Mass, weight and gravity
notes.intro: Mass and weight are not the same thing. Weight depends on gravity.
points: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).
Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, measured in newtons (N).
A newton meter (force meter) measures weight.
A hypothesis predicts what will happen and gives a scientific reason.
The independent variable is what you change; the dependent variable is what you measure.

terms.meaning: Pull of gravity on a mass, in N

notes.example: A 2 kg bag of rice has the same mass everywhere, but it would weigh less on the Moon.

notes.title: Processing results
notes.intro: Repeat readings and averages make results more reliable.
points: Add up the repeat readings and divide by how many there are to get the mean.
Give the mean with its unit and the same number of decimal places as the readings.
Plot the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis.
Label each axis with its quantity and unit.
If the points lie in a line through 0, the two quantities are proportional.

terms.meaning: When one doubles, the other doubles

notes.example: Readings 4 N, 5 N and 6 N have a mean of 15 ÷ 3 = 5 N.

notes.title: Conclusions and evaluation
notes.intro: A good conclusion answers the research question using data.
points: Describe the pattern: as one quantity increases, what does the other do?
Quote at least two pairs of numbers as evidence.
Explain the pattern with science, not just describe it.
Say whether the hypothesis was supported, and give the evidence.
Name a real source of error and an improvement that fixes it.

terms.meaning: An answer to the research question backed by data
Something that made readings less accurate
A change that makes results more reliable

notes.example: Weak: 'it was wrong.' Better: 'the pointer was moving, so wait until it stops before reading.'

notes.title: Measuring mass
notes.intro: Scientists measure mass with an electronic balance and always use units.
points: Place the balance on a flat, steady surface.
Press zero (tare) so it reads 0.0 g before adding anything.
Read the display only when the number stops changing.
1 kilogram (kg) = 1000 grams (g).
To change kg to g multiply by 1000; to change g to kg divide by 1000.

terms.meaning: The label that says what was measured, e.g. g

notes.title: Measuring volume of liquids and solids
notes.intro: Volume is the amount of space something takes up.
points: Use a measuring cylinder for liquids; units are mL or cm³ (1 mL = 1 cm³).
Water curves at the surface; this curve is the meniscus.
Read from the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with the surface.
For an irregular solid, use displacement: note the water level before and after adding it.
Volume of object = new level − starting level.

terms.meaning: The curved surface of a liquid
Water pushed up by an object put in it
Wrong reading from looking at a scale at an angle

notes.example: Water rises from 40 mL to 47 mL, so the object's volume is 7 cm³.

notes.title: Mass is not weight
notes.intro: In everyday talk we mix them up, but in science they are different.
points: Mass is how much matter an object has; it does not change from place to place.
Weight is the pull of gravity on the object; it is a force measured in newtons.
Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth of Earth's.
So on the Moon your mass is the same but your weight is smaller.

terms.meaning: Force that pulls masses towards each other
Anything that has mass and takes up space

notes.example: A 60 kg astronaut weighs about 600 N on Earth and only about 100 N on the Moon.

notes.title: Density: floating and sinking
notes.intro: Whether something floats depends on how much mass is packed into its volume.
points: Density = mass ÷ volume, measured in g/cm³.
Water has a density of 1 g/cm³.
Objects less dense than water float; objects more dense sink.
Big does not mean heavy for its size: a large log floats, a small stone sinks.
Always make a prediction before testing, then compare.

terms.meaning: Stay at the surface of a liquid
Fall to the bottom of a liquid

notes.example: An object of 30 g and 60 cm³ has density 0.5 g/cm³, so it floats.

notes.title: Density basics
notes.intro: Density tells us how tightly packed the matter in a material is.
points: Formula: density (ρ) = mass (m) ÷ volume (V).
Mass in grams and volume in cm³ give density in g/cm³.
Compare any density with water (1.0 g/cm³) to predict floating or sinking.
Always quote both numbers when you explain, not just 'it is light'.
notes.example: Oil has density 0.9 g/cm³; it is less than 1.0, so it floats on water.

notes.title: Calculating volume and density
notes.intro: Regular shapes and irregular shapes need different methods to find volume.
points: Cube: volume = side × side × side.
Cuboid: volume = length × width × height.
Irregular object: use water displacement in a measuring cylinder.
Then divide mass by volume to get density.
Show each step: formula, numbers, answer and unit.

terms.meaning: A box shape with rectangular faces
Cubic centimetre, a unit of volume

notes.example: A box 2 cm × 3 cm × 4 cm has volume 24 cm³; if its mass is 48 g, density = 2 g/cm³.

notes.title: Mixtures in real life
notes.intro: Many everyday materials are mixtures, even when they look like one substance.
points: A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined.
Homogeneous mixtures look the same all the way through, e.g. salt water.
Heterogeneous mixtures have parts you can see or detect, e.g. sand in water.
A microscope can show that something smooth-looking is really heterogeneous.
A chemical change makes new substances; mixing does not.

terms.meaning: A change that makes new substances

notes.example: Fruit salad is heterogeneous; sugar dissolved in tea is homogeneous.

notes.title: Changes of state around us
notes.intro: Matter changes state when energy is taken in or given out.
points: Melting: solid → liquid; freezing: liquid → solid.
Evaporating/boiling: liquid → gas; condensing: gas → liquid.
Sublimation: solid → gas directly; deposition: gas → solid directly.
Heating gives particles energy; cooling takes it away.
Each change has an opposite change.

terms.meaning: Solid turning straight into a gas
Gas turning straight into a solid

notes.example: Wet clothes dry in the sun because water evaporates into the air.

notes.title: Writing a hypothesis
notes.intro: A hypothesis is a testable prediction with a scientific reason.
points: Use the pattern: If… (change), then… (result), because… (science reason).
The 'if' part names the independent variable.
The 'then' part names the dependent variable and the direction of change.
The 'because' part uses scientific ideas, such as particles and energy.
A hypothesis can be supported or not supported by results.

terms.meaning: A testable prediction with a reason
Can be checked by an experiment

notes.example: If I put the plant in more light, then it will grow taller, because it can make more food.

notes.title: Safety and variables in a plan
notes.intro: A good plan keeps people safe and makes the test fair.
points: A hazard is something that could cause harm; a precaution reduces the risk.
Hot liquids, broken glass, spills and tasting are common hazards.
Change only one variable (independent) and measure one (dependent).
Keep everything else the same (controlled variables).
Repeat the test to make results more reliable.
notes.example: Hazard: hot kettle. Precaution: the teacher pours, and students stand back.

notes.title: Testing for purity
notes.intro: A pure substance contains only one kind of particle. Impure substances contain more than one.
points: Evaporating a sample can show what was dissolved in it.
A pure liquid like distilled water leaves no residue.
Tap water and salt water leave residues because they contain dissolved solids.
Plan with a research question, a prediction and clear variables.
Use the same amount and the same drying time for a fair test.
notes.example: Sea water leaves white salt crystals after it dries, so it is impure.

notes.title: Purity in everyday life
notes.intro: Many things called 'pure' in adverts are not pure in science.
points: In science, pure means one substance only.
Pure substances melt and boil at fixed, exact temperatures.
Impure substances melt or boil over a range of temperatures.
Density is another way to check a substance.
Alloys such as most gold jewellery are mixtures of metals.

terms.meaning: Temperature where a solid turns liquid
Measure of gold purity; 24 carat is pure

notes.example: Pure water boils at 100 °C; salty water boils at a higher temperature.

notes.title: Choosing a separation method
notes.intro: Mixtures can be separated because their parts have different properties.
points: Magnetic separation removes magnetic metals such as iron.
Sieving separates particles of different sizes.
Winnowing uses moving air to blow away light parts like husks.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
Decanting means carefully pouring the liquid off a settled solid.

terms.meaning: Liquid that passes through a filter
Solid left in the filter paper

notes.example: Muddy water can be filtered: the mud stays on the paper.

notes.title: Separating in several steps
notes.intro: Some mixtures need more than one method, used in a sensible order.
points: Look at each part of the mixture and its property: size, magnetism, mass, solubility.
Remove the easiest part first.
Choose a method that matches each property.
Write steps clearly, naming the equipment for each step.
Check that each step leaves the other parts unchanged.

terms.meaning: A feature of a material, e.g. magnetic
The way you do something step by step

notes.example: Rice with stones and dust: sieve out dust, then pick or wash out stones.

notes.title: Investigating dissolving
notes.intro: Dissolving speed depends on several factors you can test.
points: A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution.
Warmer solvent usually dissolves a solute faster.
Stirring and smaller grains also speed up dissolving.
Change one factor, measure the time, keep the others the same.
Write a method in numbered steps with amounts and units.
notes.example: Sugar in tea: sugar is the solute, the hot water is the solvent.

notes.title: Can it be squashed?
notes.intro: Solids, liquids and gases behave differently when pushed.
points: Gas particles are far apart, so a gas can be squashed (compressed).
Liquid particles are touching, so a liquid hardly squashes.
Solid particles are packed tightly in a fixed pattern.
A fair test uses the same push on each sample.
notes.example: A bicycle pump squashes air into a tyre.

notes.title: Particles on the move
notes.intro: Particles in liquids and gases are always moving on their own.
points: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from where there are many to where there are few.
It happens without stirring because particles move randomly.
Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids.
Warmer particles move faster, so diffusion is faster.

terms.meaning: Spreading of particles from high to low concentration

notes.example: The smell of food cooking spreads to the next room.

notes.title: Comparing solids, liquids and gases
notes.intro: Each state of matter has its own set of properties.
points: Solids keep their own shape and volume.
Liquids flow and take the shape of the container but keep their volume.
Gases fill the whole container and can be squashed.
The state at room temperature depends on the substance.
notes.example: Ice is solid, water liquid and steam gas: the same substance in three states.

notes.title: Variables in an investigation
notes.intro: Every fair test has three kinds of variable.
points: Independent variable: the one you change on purpose.
Dependent variable: the one you measure.
Controlled variables: everything you keep the same.
Always include units, such as cm³ or seconds.
Controls matter because they stop other factors from affecting the result.
notes.example: Testing how ramp height affects speed: height is changed, speed is measured.

notes.title: Calculating a mean
notes.intro: Repeating a test and taking the mean gives a more reliable result.
points: Add all the trial results together.
Divide by the number of trials.
Round to the same number of decimal places as the data.
Leave out any clear anomaly before averaging.

terms.meaning: A result that does not fit the pattern

notes.title: Describing patterns and reliability
notes.intro: Data tell a story when you describe and check them.
points: Start with 'As the … increased, the … increased/decreased'.
Use numbers from your table as evidence.
Check if the relationship is proportional: does doubling one double the other?
Repeats help spot mistakes and make the mean more reliable.
notes.example: As the temperature increased, the dissolving time decreased from 60 s to 20 s.

notes.title: Carbohydrate-rich foods
notes.intro: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy. Some foods are much richer in them than others.
points: Starchy foods such as rice, maize (ugali), bread, potatoes and cassava are rich in carbohydrate.
Sugary foods such as honey, fruit and sweets contain simple sugars.
Meat, fish, eggs and oils contain little or no carbohydrate.
Read food labels: carbohydrate is given in grams per 100 g.

terms.meaning: A complex carbohydrate made of many glucose units

notes.example: 100 g of cooked rice contains about 28 g of carbohydrate; 100 g of chicken has almost none.

notes.title: What carbohydrates do
notes.intro: Carbohydrates have several jobs in plants and animals.
points: Glucose is broken down in respiration to release energy.
Starch is the energy store in plants; glycogen is the store in animals.
Cellulose builds plant cell walls and gives fibre in our diet.
Fibre keeps food moving through the gut.

terms.meaning: A simple sugar used in respiration
Energy store in liver and muscle

notes.example: A runner eats pasta before a race to build up glycogen stores.

notes.title: Building blocks of food molecules
notes.intro: Large food molecules are built from smaller units.
points: Carbohydrates such as starch are built from sugar units like glucose.
Proteins are built from amino acids.
Lipids (fats and oils) are built from fatty acids and glycerol.
Lipids store energy and insulate the body; they also form cell membranes.

terms.meaning: Small molecule joined to fatty acids in lipids

notes.example: Digestion breaks proteins in beans into amino acids that the body can absorb.

notes.title: Matching foods to molecules
notes.intro: Most meals provide a mix of molecules, but each food is rich in one main type.
points: Cereals and tubers mainly provide carbohydrate.
Beans, lentils, meat, fish and eggs mainly provide protein.
Oils, butter and nuts mainly provide lipids.
A balanced meal contains all three.

terms.meaning: A substance in food the body needs
Contains each nutrient in the right amount

notes.example: Chapati (carbohydrate), egg (protein) and avocado (lipid).

notes.title: Fixing an unbalanced meal
notes.intro: If a meal is missing a nutrient, add a food that is rich in it.
points: First identify which molecules each food provides.
Then find the missing group.
Choose a local, affordable food that supplies it.
Explain the job of that nutrient in the body.

terms.meaning: Not getting enough of a nutrient

notes.example: Ugali and sukuma wiki lack protein: add beans or fish.

notes.title: Comparing the three big molecules
notes.intro: Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids differ in their units, jobs and food sources.
points: Carbohydrates: sugar units; quick energy; cereals and fruit.
Proteins: amino acids; growth, repair, enzymes; beans and meat.
Lipids: fatty acids and glycerol; energy store, insulation, membranes; oils and nuts.
A comparison table should use the same headings for each molecule.

terms.meaning: A protein that speeds up reactions

notes.example: Per gram, lipids give about twice as much energy as carbohydrates.

notes.title: pH and enzymes
notes.intro: Each enzyme works best at one pH, called its optimum pH.
points: pH measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is (0–14; 7 is neutral).
Away from the optimum, the enzyme works more slowly.
Strong acid or alkali changes the shape of the active site.
When the active site changes shape the enzyme is denatured: the substrate no longer fits.
Use figures from the results to describe patterns.

terms.meaning: The pH at which an enzyme works fastest
The part of the enzyme the substrate fits into
Active site permanently changed in shape

notes.example: Pepsin in the stomach works best at about pH 2; amylase in saliva at about pH 7.

notes.title: Graphing enzyme results
notes.intro: A graph shows an enzyme's activity across a range of conditions.
points: Put the independent variable (pH) on the x-axis.
Put the dependent variable (e.g. foam height) on the y-axis with units.
Plot points accurately and join them with a smooth curve or straight lines.
The highest point of the curve shows the optimum.
notes.example: A bell-shaped curve with a peak at pH 7 shows an optimum of pH 7.

notes.title: Energy stored in food
notes.intro: Food contains chemical energy that can be released by burning.
points: Burning food is a chemical reaction that transfers chemical energy to thermal energy.
The thermal energy heats the water above the food.
The bigger the temperature rise, the more energy was released.
Energy is transferred, not created or destroyed.

terms.meaning: Energy stored in the bonds of molecules

notes.example: A peanut burning under a boiling tube heats the water by several degrees.

notes.title: Planning a calorimetry test
notes.intro: To compare foods fairly you must control the conditions.
points: Independent variable: the type of food.
Dependent variable: temperature rise of the water (°C).
Controls: same mass of food, same volume of water, same distance from the flame.
Heat loss to the air is the main source of error.

terms.meaning: Equipment used to measure energy released

notes.example: Use 20 cm³ of water and 1 g of each food every time.

notes.title: Calculating energy from food
notes.intro: We can calculate the energy released using the water's temperature rise.
points: Energy (J) = mass of water (g) × 4.2 × temperature rise (°C).
4.2 J heats 1 g of water by 1 °C.
Divide by the mass of food to get energy per gram (J/g).
Divide by 1000 to change J into kJ.

terms.meaning: Energy to heat 1 g of a substance by 1 °C

notes.example: 20 g water rising 10 °C: 20 × 4.2 × 10 = 840 J.

notes.title: Evaluating energy results
notes.intro: Results from burning food are always lower than the true values.
points: Compare energy per gram between foods, not total energy.
Lipid-rich foods release the most energy per gram.
Much heat escapes to the air and the tube, so measured values are too low.
Improvements: insulate the tube, keep the food close, relight if it goes out.

terms.meaning: Error that pushes all results the same way
Judge how good the method and results are

notes.example: Food labels show peanuts at about 2500 kJ per 100 g, much more than a school test gives.

notes.title: Substrate concentration and rate
notes.intro: Adding more substrate speeds up an enzyme reaction, but only up to a point.
points: At low substrate concentration, many active sites are empty, so adding substrate raises the rate.
At high concentration, all active sites are busy (saturated).
Then the rate stays the same: the graph levels off.
The limit is now the number of enzyme molecules.

terms.meaning: The molecule an enzyme acts on
The factor that stops the rate rising

notes.example: A shop with 3 tills: more customers helps until all tills are busy.

notes.title: Reading enzyme graphs
notes.intro: Enzyme graphs for temperature, pH and enzyme concentration have different shapes.
points: Temperature: rate rises as particles move faster, then falls steeply as the enzyme denatures.
pH: a peak at the optimum, falling either side.
Enzyme concentration: with plenty of substrate, rate rises in a straight line.
Read the optimum from the x-value of the peak.

terms.meaning: Temperature at which rate is highest

notes.example: Human enzymes usually have an optimum of about 37 °C.

notes.title: Enzymes in industry and the home
notes.intro: Enzymes are used to make products faster and at lower temperatures.
points: Biological washing powders contain proteases (break down protein stains) and lipases (break down fat stains).
Amylase breaks starch into sugars for syrups and brewing.
Pectinase helps get juice out of fruit.
Enzymes work at low temperatures, saving energy and money.
notes.example: Rennet (chymosin) is used to make cheese by clotting milk.

notes.title: Temperature and washing
notes.intro: Washing powder enzymes depend on the right temperature.
points: Warmer water gives particles more kinetic energy, so more collisions with active sites.
Too hot, and the enzyme's active site changes shape: it is denatured.
Denaturing is permanent; the enzyme cannot work again.
Labels give a temperature range for best results.

terms.meaning: Change the shape of an enzyme so it stops working

notes.example: Boiling an egg changes its protein for good: it cannot become runny again.

notes.title: Catalase in potato
notes.intro: Catalase is an enzyme found in most living cells, including potato.
points: Hydrogen peroxide is a harmful waste product in cells.
Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen.
The oxygen gas makes bubbles or foam.
The substrate fits into the enzyme's active site.

terms.meaning: Enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide

notes.example: Pouring peroxide on a cut makes it fizz because blood contains catalase.

notes.title: Enzymes in everyday products
notes.intro: The same ideas from the lab explain how enzyme products work.
points: Each enzyme acts on one substrate only (specificity).
Proteases remove protein stains like blood and egg.
Lipases remove grease and oil stains.
Amylases remove starch stains like gravy.

terms.meaning: Each enzyme works on one substrate
Mark left by food or other substances

notes.example: A grass stain contains protein, so a protease helps remove it.

notes.title: Lock and key model
notes.intro: The lock and key model explains why an enzyme only works on one substrate.
points: The enzyme is like a lock; its active site is the keyhole.
The substrate is like the key; it must fit the active site exactly.
A substrate with the wrong shape cannot bind.
After the reaction the products leave and the enzyme can be used again.

terms.meaning: A simple picture that explains a real thing

notes.example: Amylase fits starch but not fat, just as one key opens only one lock.

notes.title: Digestive enzymes
notes.intro: Digestive enzymes break large food molecules into small ones the body can absorb.
points: Amylase: starch → sugars (mouth, small intestine).
Protease: proteins → amino acids (stomach, small intestine).
Lipase: lipids → fatty acids and glycerol (small intestine).
Each enzyme's active site matches only its own substrate.

terms.meaning: Breaking food into small soluble molecules
Taking digested food into the blood

notes.example: Chewing bread for a long time makes it taste sweet as amylase makes sugar.

notes.title: Means and anomalies
notes.intro: Repeats help you find anomalies and calculate reliable means.
points: An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern of the others.
Spot it by comparing repeats: one is much bigger or smaller.
Leave the anomaly out when calculating the mean.
Say how you decided it was anomalous.

terms.meaning: Same person, same method, similar results

notes.example: Repeats of 12, 13 and 25 s: 25 s is the anomaly; mean = 12.5 s.

notes.title: Describing enzyme temperature graphs
notes.intro: Enzyme activity rises and then falls as temperature increases.
points: Describe both parts of the curve: the rise and the fall.
Quote figures from your results for each part.
The optimum is the temperature at the peak.
Explain using collisions (rise) and denaturing (fall).
notes.example: Rate rises from 10 °C to 40 °C, then drops sharply by 60 °C.

notes.title: Testing for starch
notes.intro: Iodine solution is used to test foods for starch.
points: Add a few drops of iodine solution to the food.
Iodine starts orange-brown.
If starch is present, it turns blue-black.
If it stays orange-brown, starch is absent.

terms.meaning: A chemical used in a test

notes.example: A slice of potato turns blue-black with iodine.

notes.title: Positive, negative and controls
notes.intro: Food tests rely on colour changes, and controls make them trustworthy.
points: A positive result shows the nutrient is present.
A negative result means no colour change.
A control (distilled water) shows what 'no nutrient' looks like.
Controls help spot contaminated reagents.

terms.meaning: A test without the substance, for comparison

notes.example: If the distilled water turns blue-black with iodine, the dropper is dirty.

notes.title: Interpreting a results table
notes.intro: A table of food test results shows which nutrients each food contains.
points: Count the positive results in each row.
Compare samples side by side for one nutrient.
A stronger colour can mean more of the nutrient (e.g. DCPIP decolourises faster).
Use results as evidence in your answers.

terms.meaning: Blue reagent that loses its colour with vitamin C

notes.example: Orange juice decolourises DCPIP quickly, so it is rich in vitamin C.

notes.title: Explaining unexpected results
notes.intro: Sometimes results seem surprising; science explains why.
points: Benedict's test detects reducing sugars and needs heating in a water bath.
Without heating, Benedict's stays blue.
Starch is not a reducing sugar, so it gives a negative Benedict's test.
Non-reducing sugars like sucrose need extra steps first.

terms.meaning: Sugar such as glucose that reacts with Benedict's
Container of hot water for heating tubes

notes.example: Benedict's changes blue → green → yellow → orange → brick-red as sugar increases.

notes.title: Joining and splitting molecules
notes.intro: Small molecules join and split using water.
points: When two small molecules join, a water molecule is released: condensation reaction.
When water is used to split a large molecule: hydrolysis.
Evaporation turns liquid to gas; condensation turns gas to liquid (water cycle).
The word 'condensation' is used in both, but means different things.
notes.example: Two glucose molecules join to form maltose and one water molecule.

notes.title: Monomer, dimer, polymer
notes.intro: Many biological molecules are chains of repeating units.
points: Mono = one, di = two, poly = many.
A monomer is one small unit, such as glucose.
A dimer is two units joined, such as maltose.
A polymer is a long chain of many units, such as starch.

terms.meaning: Many units joined in a chain

notes.example: Beads: one bead = monomer, two beads = dimer, a necklace = polymer.

notes.title: Three glucose polymers
notes.intro: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of glucose but do different jobs.
points: Starch: energy store in plants (seeds, tubers).
Glycogen: energy store in animals (liver, muscles).
Cellulose: strong fibres in plant cell walls.
Their properties differ because the glucose units are joined in different ways.

terms.meaning: Strong layer outside a plant cell

notes.example: Cassava stores starch; your liver stores glycogen; cotton is mostly cellulose.

notes.title: Food groups
notes.intro: A balanced diet includes foods from every group.
points: Carbohydrates: energy (maize, rice, bread).
Proteins: growth and repair (beans, fish, eggs).
Lipids: stored energy and insulation (oil, nuts).
Vitamins and minerals: keep the body healthy (fruit, vegetables).
Fibre and water: digestion and body functions.

terms.meaning: Diet with too much or too little of a nutrient

notes.example: Rice with beans, vegetables and fruit covers most food groups.

notes.title: Evidence for photosynthesis
notes.intro: Experiments show where plants get their mass and what they give off.
points: Van Helmont found a tree gained much more mass than the soil lost.
Most plant mass comes from carbon dioxide and water, not soil.
Pondweed gives off bubbles of oxygen in light.
Closer lamp → brighter light → more bubbles.

terms.meaning: Making glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light

notes.example: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy, chlorophyll).

notes.title: Limiting factors of photosynthesis
notes.intro: Light, carbon dioxide and temperature all affect the rate of photosynthesis.
points: More light increases the rate up to a point.
Then something else limits it, such as carbon dioxide or temperature.
Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes.
Too high a temperature denatures the enzymes and the rate falls.

terms.meaning: The factor in shortest supply that holds the rate back

notes.example: Greenhouses add warmth and CO₂ so crops grow faster.

notes.title: Respiration
notes.intro: Respiration releases energy from glucose in every living cell.
points: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and gives carbon dioxide and water.
It happens in the mitochondria.
The energy is used for movement, growth, keeping warm and active transport.
Respiration is not breathing; it happens in cells, day and night.
notes.example: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released).

notes.title: Building proteins
notes.intro: Proteins are long chains built from amino acids.
points: There are 20 different amino acids.
Amino acids join by peptide bonds in a condensation reaction.
The order of amino acids decides the protein's shape.
The shape decides the protein's job.
notes.example: Like letters making different words, amino acids in different orders make different proteins.

notes.title: Sources of protein
notes.intro: Protein comes from both plants and animals.
points: Animal sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk.
Plant sources: beans, lentils, groundnuts, soya.
Many foods supply protein and another nutrient together.
Mixing plant proteins gives all the amino acids we need.

terms.meaning: Amino acids the body cannot make

notes.example: Milk gives protein and calcium; groundnuts give protein and lipid.

notes.title: Jobs of proteins
notes.intro: Proteins do many jobs in the body.
points: Growth and repair of tissues such as muscle and skin.
Enzymes that speed up reactions.
Hormones such as insulin.
Antibodies that fight infection.
Transport, such as haemoglobin carrying oxygen.

terms.meaning: Protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen

notes.example: A lack of protein in children can cause kwashiorkor.

notes.title: Planning the temperature experiment
notes.intro: A clear hypothesis and variables make the investigation fair.
points: Predict the pattern and give a reason using enzyme ideas.
Independent variable: temperature (°C).
Dependent variable: height of foam (mm or cm).
Controls: same volume of peroxide, same mass of potato, same time.

terms.meaning: Keeps tubes at a set temperature

notes.example: If temperature rises to 40 °C, foam will rise, because molecules collide more often.

notes.title: Pooling class results
notes.intro: Sharing results across groups gives more data and more reliable means.
points: Each group tests one temperature, so the class covers the whole range.
Several groups at the same temperature give repeats.
Pooled data are more reliable but depend on everyone using the same method.
Differences between groups can cause anomalies.
notes.example: Five groups at 40 °C give five repeats for that temperature.

notes.title: Analysing temperature results
notes.intro: Calculate means, plot a graph and explain the shape.
points: Calculate the mean for each temperature without anomalies.
Plot temperature on the x-axis and mean foam height on the y-axis.
Describe the rise, the peak (optimum) and the fall with figures.
Explain the rise with more collisions and the fall with denaturing.

terms.meaning: Permanent change in active site shape

notes.example: Foam might rise from 10 mm at 10 °C to 40 mm at 40 °C, then fall to 5 mm at 70 °C.

notes.title: Evaluating the experiment
notes.intro: Evaluation looks at whether results support the hypothesis and how to improve.
points: State yes or no for the hypothesis and quote data.
Identify any anomaly and suggest a cause (e.g. timing, temperature not reached).
Suggest improvements: smaller temperature steps, more repeats, a thermometer in each tube.
Limitations reduce confidence in the conclusion.

terms.meaning: Whether the test measures what it should

notes.example: Test every 5 °C near the peak to find the optimum more precisely.

notes.title: Nutrients and their jobs
notes.intro: Each nutrient in food has a main job in the body.
points: Carbohydrates: main source of energy.
Proteins: growth and repair.
Lipids: energy store and insulation.
Vitamins and minerals: healthy body processes.
Fibre: helps food move through the gut.

terms.meaning: Substance in food needed by the body

notes.example: Iron (a mineral) helps make red blood cells.

notes.title: Foods with more than one nutrient
notes.intro: Most foods contain a mix of nutrients.
points: Beans contain both protein and carbohydrate.
Milk contains protein, lipid and calcium.
Lipids include both solid fats and liquid oils.
Oils are lipids because of their chemical make-up, not their state.

terms.meaning: Lipid that is solid at room temperature
Lipid that is liquid at room temperature

notes.example: Butter is a solid lipid; sunflower oil is a liquid lipid.

notes.title: Reading food labels
notes.intro: Food labels tell us what nutrients are in food and how much.
points: Values are usually given per 100 g and per serving.
Compare foods using the per 100 g column.
Look at energy (kJ), carbohydrate, sugar, protein, fat and salt.
Use labels to plan a balanced diet.

terms.meaning: An amount of food usually eaten at once

notes.example: A cereal with 30 g sugar per 100 g is high in sugar.

notes.title: Are viruses alive?
notes.intro: Viruses are on the border between living and non-living.
points: Viruses are made of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat.
They have no cytoplasm, cell membrane or ribosomes.
They cannot carry out metabolism on their own.
To reproduce, a virus must enter a host cell and use the host's ribosomes and enzymes.
Viruses are much smaller than bacteria.

terms.meaning: Non-cellular particle of genes in a protein coat
Cell a virus infects and uses

notes.example: The influenza virus uses cells in your airways to make thousands of new viruses.

notes.title: Plant and animal cell structures
notes.intro: Animal and plant cells share some structures, and plant cells have extra ones.
points: Both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.
Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall.
Plant cells have chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Plant cells have a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap.

terms.meaning: A structure inside a cell with a specific job
Rigid outer layer of plant cells

notes.example: An onion skin cell has a cell wall and vacuole but no chloroplasts, because it is underground.

notes.title: What each organelle does
notes.intro: Each organelle has a job that helps the cell survive.
points: Nucleus: contains DNA and controls the cell.
Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves.
Mitochondria: site of aerobic respiration.
Ribosomes: make proteins.
Chloroplasts: absorb light for photosynthesis.
notes.example: A cell is like a school: the nucleus is the head teacher's office giving instructions.

notes.title: Inside mitochondria and chloroplasts
notes.intro: Both organelles have double membranes and folded inner structures.
points: Mitochondria have an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane (cristae).
The matrix is the fluid inside the mitochondrion.
Chloroplasts contain stacks of thylakoids called grana, surrounded by stroma.
Chlorophyll in the thylakoids absorbs light.
Folds and stacks increase surface area for reactions.

terms.meaning: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane

notes.example: More folds means more space for enzymes, like adding shelves to a cupboard.

notes.title: Organelles and cell jobs
notes.intro: The number of each organelle matches the job of the cell.
points: Cells needing lots of energy have many mitochondria.
Cells making lots of protein have many ribosomes.
Leaf cells in sunlight have many chloroplasts.
Read statements carefully: check which cell type each organelle is found in.

terms.meaning: Feature that helps a cell or organism do its job
Cell with structure suited to a job

notes.example: Sperm cells have many mitochondria in the midpiece to power swimming.

notes.title: The cell theory
notes.intro: Cell theory is one of the big ideas of biology, built by many scientists.
points: All living things are made of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function.
All cells come from pre-existing cells.
Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39) proposed the first two ideas; Virchow added the third (1855).
The third idea replaced the old belief that life could appear from non-living matter.

terms.meaning: A well-tested explanation supported by evidence
Old idea that life arises from non-living things

notes.example: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment supported the idea that cells come only from cells.

notes.title: The cell as a factory
notes.intro: Analogies help us remember organelle jobs, but every analogy has limits.
points: Nucleus: like a control office holding the plans (DNA).
Ribosomes: like workers assembling products (proteins).
Rough ER: like a conveyor belt moving proteins.
Golgi apparatus: like the packaging and shipping department.
Mitochondria: like the power station.

terms.meaning: A comparison that explains an idea

notes.example: A mitochondrion does not make energy like a power station; it releases energy from glucose.

notes.title: Responsible investigation
notes.intro: Investigating living things raises ethical questions as well as scientific ones.
points: Consider arguments on both sides of an issue before deciding.
Respect for living organisms: minimise harm and use the fewest organisms needed.
Safety: follow risk assessments for microbes and chemicals.
Honesty: record real data, including unexpected results.
A good plan states a research question, variables and method.

terms.meaning: Ideas about what is right and wrong

notes.example: Use a plant cell (onion) instead of animal tissue when either would answer the question.

notes.title: The seven characteristics of life
notes.intro: MRS GREN helps you remember what all living things do.
points: Movement: changing position or moving parts.
Respiration: releasing energy from food in cells.
Sensitivity: detecting and responding to changes.
Growth: a permanent increase in size or mass.
Reproduction, Excretion (removing waste) and Nutrition (getting food).

terms.meaning: Removing waste made by the body's reactions

notes.example: A sunflower turning towards light shows sensitivity.

notes.title: Applying MRS GREN
notes.intro: Something is living only if it shows all seven characteristics.
points: Some non-living things show one characteristic, such as a moving car.
Crystals can 'grow' but they do not respire or reproduce.
Seeds and spores may look inactive but are alive.
Check every characteristic before deciding.

terms.meaning: A change that an organism detects
Alive but inactive, e.g. a seed

notes.example: Fire moves, grows and uses oxygen, but it is not made of cells, so it is not alive.

notes.title: Improving an answer
notes.intro: Correcting your own work is a powerful way to learn.
points: Find the question where you lost marks.
Compare your answer with the key ideas: are scientific words used?
Rewrite it with a clear claim, evidence and a reason.
Check you answered the command word (state, describe, explain).

terms.meaning: Word telling you what kind of answer is needed

notes.example: Instead of 'it grows', write 'it shows growth because its mass permanently increases'.

notes.title: Prokaryotes versus eukaryotes
notes.intro: All cells are either prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
points: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus; their DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm.
Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi) have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.
Prokaryotes may have plasmids, a flagellum and a cell wall not made of cellulose.
Prokaryotic cells are much smaller.

terms.meaning: Small ring of extra DNA in bacteria

notes.example: E. coli is a prokaryote; a human cheek cell is a eukaryote.

notes.title: Thinking about the first cells
notes.intro: Scientists use evidence to explain how complex cells may have arisen.
points: Prokaryotes appeared first, over 3.5 billion years ago.
Endosymbiosis: mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes.
Evidence: they have their own DNA, ribosomes and double membranes.
A good answer links a claim to evidence and reasoning.
notes.example: Mitochondria divide on their own, like bacteria do.

notes.title: Identifying cell types
notes.intro: Use visible structures as evidence to identify a cell.
points: No nucleus → prokaryote (bacterium).
Nucleus + cell wall + chloroplasts → plant cell.
Nucleus, no cell wall → animal cell.
Nucleus + chitin cell wall, no chloroplasts → fungal cell.
Always name the structure you used as evidence.

terms.meaning: Region with DNA in a prokaryote

notes.example: A cell with a nucleus and a wall but no chloroplasts could be a root cell or a fungus: look closer.

notes.title: Specialized cells
notes.intro: Cells have special structures that match their jobs.
points: Root hair cells have long extensions that increase surface area for absorbing water.
Red blood cells have no nucleus and a biconcave shape to carry more oxygen.
Nerve cells are long to carry impulses over distances.
Muscle and sperm cells have many mitochondria for energy.

terms.meaning: Total area of the outside of something

notes.example: Villi in the small intestine have microvilli to absorb more digested food.

notes.title: Stem cells
notes.intro: Stem cells can divide and become many types of cell.
points: Stem cells are unspecialized.
Differentiation is the process of becoming specialized.
Embryonic stem cells can become almost any cell type.
Adult stem cells (e.g. in bone marrow) make a limited range of cells.
Link structure → adaptation → function in a chain.

terms.meaning: Unspecialized cell that can divide and differentiate

notes.example: Bone marrow stem cells make red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

notes.title: Using evidence about cells
notes.intro: Exam questions often give data about unknown cells.
points: Look for clues: shape, size, organelles, surface area.
Thin and flat suits diffusion over short distances.
A stem cell often has a large nucleus and few special features.
Link each feature to its job using 'which means' or 'so that'.

terms.meaning: Movement from high to low concentration
Feature or data you use to support an answer

notes.example: Alveolus cells are very thin, so gases diffuse a short distance.

notes.title: Surface area and volume of cubes
notes.intro: Cubes are simple models of cells.
points: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side × side.
Volume of a cube = side × side × side.
SA : V ratio = surface area ÷ volume.
As the cube grows, volume increases faster than surface area.
So the SA : V ratio gets smaller.
notes.example: A 1 cm cube: SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, ratio 6 : 1.

notes.title: Why cells stay small
notes.intro: The SA : V ratio limits how big a cell can be.
points: Substances enter and leave through the cell surface.
The whole volume of the cell needs those substances.
A large cell has less surface for each unit of volume.
Diffusion to the centre takes too long in a large cell.
Small cells or flat, folded shapes keep the ratio high.

terms.meaning: How far a substance must travel
Taking in and giving out substances

notes.example: Large organisms use lungs and blood vessels because diffusion alone is too slow.

notes.title: Applying SA : V ratio
notes.intro: Use calculations and data to compare cell models.
points: Calculate SA and V carefully with units (cm² and cm³).
The highest ratio means the most efficient exchange.
Check which statements the data actually support.
Shapes that are flat or long have a high ratio even when large.

terms.meaning: Doing a job well with little waste

notes.example: A 2 cm cube: SA = 24 cm², V = 8 cm³, ratio 3 : 1.

notes.title: Hooke and early microscopes
notes.intro: The microscope opened up the world of cells.
points: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at thin slices of cork.
He saw tiny boxes and called them 'cells', like rooms in a monastery.
Cork cells are dead, so only the cell walls remained.
Leeuwenhoek's better lenses let him see living microbes.
Better technology leads to new discoveries.

terms.meaning: How many times bigger an image is

notes.example: Leeuwenhoek called the microbes he saw in pond water 'animalcules'.

notes.title: Cell theory as a model
notes.intro: Cell theory is a model that connects all living things.
points: A timeline shows how ideas built up over 200 years.
Hooke (1665), Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39), Virchow (1855).
Form: all organisms are made of cells.
Relationships: every cell comes from another cell, linking all life.
Models can change when new evidence appears.
notes.example: Viruses challenge the model because they are not cells but can reproduce inside cells.

notes.title: Agar cube investigation
notes.intro: Agar cubes model how substances diffuse into cells.
points: Agar with indicator changes colour as acid or alkali diffuses in.
Cubes of different sizes are placed in the solution.
Independent variable: cube size; dependent variable: time to change colour completely.
Controls: same solution, same concentration, same temperature.

terms.meaning: Chemical that changes colour with pH

notes.example: Phenolphthalein in agar is pink in alkali and turns colourless as acid diffuses in.

notes.title: Collecting results
notes.intro: Shared results need careful measurement.
points: Time from placing the cube in the solution until no pink is left.
Record times in seconds in a table.
Results in a video may differ from a real lab because of temperature or concentration.
Repeat to improve reliability.

terms.meaning: Same results by a different person or method
Moment when the change is complete

notes.example: A 1 cm cube may clear in a few minutes; a 3 cm cube can take much longer.

notes.title: Graphing SA : V and time
notes.intro: A graph links the SA : V ratio to the diffusion time.
points: Calculate SA, V and ratio for each cube.
Plot ratio on the x-axis and time on the y-axis.
Label axes with units and draw a line or curve of best fit.
Describe the pattern: higher ratio, shorter time.

terms.meaning: A line that shows the trend through points
As one increases the other decreases

notes.example: A ratio of 6 gives the shortest time; a ratio of 2 gives the longest.

notes.title: Concluding from a model
notes.intro: Models help us explain, but they have limits.
points: Conclusion: cubes with a smaller SA : V ratio take longer to change completely.
This explains why real cells are small.
Only three cubes give little data; more sizes and repeats would help.
Agar is not alive: real cells use active transport and have organelles.

terms.meaning: Use data to predict beyond the range

notes.example: A cell the size of a football could not get oxygen to its centre fast enough.
